title: Having Weak Muscles and Excess Body Fat Dramatically Raises Your Dementia Risk — and South Asians May Be Uniquely Vulnerable
excerpt: A landmark Curtin University study of nearly 500,000 adults finds sarcopenic obesity is a major dementia driver, while being overweight alone is not — if muscle strength is preserved
body:
India's diaspora has long known that body-mass index tells an incomplete story about health. Now a sweeping study — tracking nearly half a million adults over more than a decade — adds a troubling new chapter: the combination of low muscle strength and excess body fat, a condition researchers call sarcopenic obesity, significantly raises the risk of developing dementia.

The finding, from a Curtin University research group and published in *The Lancet Healthy Longevity* this week, carries a striking corollary. Obesity on its own was **not** associated with higher dementia risk — provided muscle strength was preserved. It is the erosion of muscle, not the accumulation of fat alone, that appears to unlock the door to cognitive decline.

"There is still a widespread belief that dementia is an unavoidable part of ageing, which is not the case," said Professor Blossom Stephan, Chair in Dementia at Curtin's enAble Institute and a co-author of the research. "But even when people are aware of the risks, barriers such as time, cost and motivation can prevent them from making changes."

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

The implications are particularly pointed for South Asians. The so-called "skinny fat" phenotype — a deceptively normal BMI masking high visceral fat and low muscle mass — is well-documented in people of Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi and Sri Lankan descent. More than one-third of South Asian men and roughly 17 per cent of South Asian women have metabolic syndrome, characterised by abdominal fat accumulation, high blood sugar, elevated blood pressure and abnormal cholesterol — all while looking outwardly lean.

A separate Northwestern Medicine study published earlier this year in the *Journal of the American Heart Association* found that South Asian adults in the United States had some of the highest rates of prediabetes, diabetes and hypertension by age 45, despite reporting healthier diets, lower alcohol use and comparable exercise habits to white Americans. The researchers called the mismatch "surprising" and said it pointed to something "fundamental" that existing health paradigms are missing.

The Curtin findings now add cognitive decline to that list of under-recognised risks. For NRI families watching elderly parents or grandparents lose sharpness, the message is clear: the protective factor is not thinness — it is muscular fitness.

## The Modifiable Risk Window

The research sits within a broader body of work showing that up to 45 per cent of all dementia cases are linked to risk factors that people can change — lifestyle habits, health conditions and environmental exposures. A companion systematic review by the same team, also published in *The Lancet Healthy Longevity*, found that mass public-awareness campaigns about dementia prevention routinely fall short.

After analysing programmes across eight countries, Professor Mario Siervo, lead author from Curtin's School of Population Health, concluded that simply telling people about risks rarely leads to lasting behaviour change. What works instead are personalised risk assessments, interactive community programmes led by trusted local figures, and culturally tailored education delivered in familiar settings.

"When people understand their own personal risk and are given clear, practical ways to act — especially through trusted community networks — they are more likely to make meaningful changes," Professor Siervo said.

## What You Can Actually Do

The prescription that emerges from both studies is not a crash diet or a marathon training plan. It is, at its core, a commitment to preserving and building muscle — through any form of resistance training — alongside managing body composition. For desk-bound NRI professionals in their 40s and 50s, the evidence suggests this may be the single most important thing they can do for long-term brain health.

Strength training two to three times a week, even with bodyweight exercises, has been shown to improve grip strength, reduce visceral fat and lower systemic inflammation — all of which are now directly implicated in dementia risk. Combined with dietary adjustments to reduce refined carbohydrates and increase protein intake, these are changes well within reach of most diaspora households.

The research also reinforces a point that South Asian health advocates have been making for years: BMI is a poor proxy for metabolic health in this population. Waist-to-hip ratio, body-fat percentage and grip strength are far more informative — and the Curtin study suggests they may also be more predictive of cognitive outcomes decades later.

## A Call to Rethink Ageing

With dementia diagnoses projected to double globally between 2020 and 2060, and with South Asians already bearing a disproportionate cardiometabolic burden, the Curtin findings are both a warning and an opportunity. The warning is that the "skinny fat" profile so common in the diaspora may carry cognitive risks that have gone unmeasured. The opportunity is that muscle strength is modifiable at any age — and the window for prevention is wider than most people assume.

"We need to combine broad public messaging with targeted support that helps people take action," Professor Stephan said. "That means investing in programmes that are accessible, culturally relevant and designed with communities, not just delivered to them."

For diaspora Indians, the takeaway is personal: pick up the weights before you pick up the supplements. Your brain may depend on it.
